content.summary_of_the_paper:
In this paper, the authors study the ability of emergent communication of representing spatial relationships through randomly generating objects. In their random dataset setting, the input images for speaker and listener are different, and they are forced to communicate with the abstract spatial relationship. They further extend referential game to an image placement task to evaluate whether emergent language conveys the information completely. 

[EDIT]: After virtual meeting with other reviewers and AC chair, I decided to incorporate some of their concerns into my review as well. The really interesting aspect of this paper is communicating spatial relationship through emergent language. This might give us hint about how preposition emerges in language. However, this paper doesn't present enough interesting findings on that direction. Therefore, I decide to lower my score to 6.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
**Strength**

1. The proposed emergent communication task is very interesting. Forcing agents to communicate spatial relationship is a cool idea.
2. The image placement task is also useful for future research. Referential games always become too easy when distractors space is too small. Placement provides a large enough space to force model to use accurate and abstract language to communicate. 
3. Their finding that using pre-trained speaker for multi-step placement task is a surprising one. 

**Weakness**

 It is not clear that the model really communicates the positional relationship. For example, it is also possible that instead of relative positions, the model actually communicates the absolute positions.

content.summary_of_the_review: Good paper, although it is not clear whether the relative relationship or absolute positions are being conveyed.

> It is not clear that the model really communicates the positional relationship. For example, it is also possible that instead of relative positions, the model actually communicates the absolute positions.


Since our random image generator generates images where the absolute positions of objects vary, when using the random dataset, the objects observed by Speaker and Listener have different absolute positions, so merely communicating the absolute positions is not enough to accomplish the task.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper describes a referential game between two agents where a speaker agent must communicate a *positional* relationship between two objects (e.g. "circle above square"). The authors motivate this task by explaining that the typical Lewis referential games studied in the literature are often limited to relatively simple referring expressions (e.g. *red shape*) rather than more abstract visual concepts. Setting up a toy image generation setting where 2D shapes of different types and positional relationships are constructed, the authors describe a number of experimens where they show that agents can learn to describe positional relationships so long as different images are given to the speaker and listener agent, so that they communicate visual features that generalize across different visual inputs (note this phenomenon has been noted in the literature). Agents trained in this way exhibit much better compositionality/systematicity measures according to the various metrics in the literature, e.g. topographic similarity, transfer to image classification tasks, etc.

One of the main arguments from the authors is that learning to communicate abstract concepts might be more important for enabling more general capabilities in agents, which the authors measure by evaluating listeners on a toy MDP "Object Placement" task where the goal is to place a set of objects in a gridworld according to the positional relationship described by a frozen speaker agent, and measuring the suitability of the emergent languages for this task.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
# Strengths

- Technically, I can't find much to fault with the paper. The paper has the correct setup for an emergent communication study, the communication protocol is carefully analyzed with a variety of metrics proposed in the literature, 
- I really like the MDP transfer task, and agree that we should be testing emergent languages for transfer on tasks that are more straightforwardly useful to humans, rather than just trying to assess performance to new Lewis referential games. There are several careful baselines here (rl from scratch, image as input features, pretrained CNN as input features), which makes the results convincing and shows that the emergent languages do indeed serve as nice starting points for some multi-agent tasks.

# Weaknesses

- My biggest hesitation with this work is just whether or not these results are by themselves interesting enough to warrant an entire paper at ICLR. Many results in this paper are fairly well established. E.g. showing different images to the teacher and student has been shown to be essential to generalization of reference games as well as increased compositionality of the language. One of the original Emergent Communication papers ([Lazaridou et al., 2017](https://arxiv.org/abs/1612.07182)) shows this, and this has been replicated in [Bouchacort and Baroni, 2018](https://arxiv.org/abs/1808.10696), [Dessi et al., 2021](https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.04258), etc. [Mu and Goodman, 2022](https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.02668) also find this property emerging in reference games, and also suggest the idea of reference games encoding more abstract concepts (e.g. boolean combinations of features), bringing me to my next point.
- I like the idea of pushing on reference games that require more abstract visual reasoning, but two-object positional relationships are a fairly limited concept, and the dataset itself is strictly a toy dataset. It would be interesting, for example, to set up a similar task with more realistic datasets, e.g. one could mine [visual genome](https://visualgenome.org/) for realistic images with real-world positional relationships, or even something slightly less abstract (yet still artificial) like [abstract scenes](http://optimus.cc.gatech.edu/clipart/). The limited scope of the emergent communication dataset also results in the fairly limited downstream tasks: I find the Object Placement MDP task interesting, but again is not really approaching the kinds of more realistic reasoning we'd want agents to do (e.g. in harder games, or in realistic navigation settings).
- I am extremely surprised at the Figure 4 SimCLR results showing that using a better image encoder is unable to generalize. These results are training on the random dataset, correct? If the dataset is randomly generated throughout training shouldn't there be *no* test distribution shift, i.e. test distribution is identical to training distribution? This also contradicts a long tradition in the literature that uses pretrained image encoders as starting points for emergent communication, e.g. the original [Lazaridou et al. (2017)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1612.07182) which uses pretrained VGG networks.

##  Minor

- How are the distractors sampled in the batch? If distractor images are randomly sampled, then quite frequently agents would not actually need to communicate the specific positional relationship, right? It seems like the strongest version of this task would more carefully sample "hard negatives" which, for example, include the same shapes as the target images, but in a different positional relationship, or alternatively has the same positional relationship with one property changed.
- Dataset terms are a little unclear. "Random dataset" is slightly misleading ---the fact that the images are "randomly generated" is not the key differentiating factor here since this is also true in the "variation dataset". Rather, the key factor is that the images given to the speaker and listener are different. Perhaps literally just call this "different image dataset"? More generally the various datasets (fixed, variation, random) could really do with a concise figure describing the differences between what these look like (e.g. with example games).
- How big is the fixed dataset? It doesn't seem to be stated. At a certain dataset size, will the fixed dataset be roughly equivalent to the variation dataset performance?
- Why are # of distractors changed from training to test time from 32 to 20? This feels like an arbitrary decision.
- Speaker is frozen in the Object Placement Transfer task, right? Did authors try additional finetuning of the speaker, using emergent communciation as the initialization point (i.e., combining "RL-scratch" with "ours")? Would that lead to bigger gains?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: See rest of review. For reproducibility, hyperparams are fairly carefully described in appendix. I hope the dataset generator and code will be made public if accepted.
content.summary_of_the_review:
To summarize, I think this paper presents a number of technically sound experiments with all the right controls and ingredients that are typical of emergent communication papers in the literature. My main concern is that the tasks and findings throughout the paper are just a little too toy and/or marginal to be of significant interest/impact to the community.

I think the papers' biggest strength is the evaluation on the MDP task. I agree with the authors' assessment that this is a much more interesting application of emergent language, i.e. does it facilitate downstream transfer to more interesting multi-agent cooperation tasks, perhaps tasks that have more practical use for humans (otherwise, I find a lot of the emergent communication literature is stuck in this local suboptimum of not being particularly useful for human-AI collaboration). For another paper along these lines see [Yao et al., 2022](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.13344). Again, it's a shame that this is a fairly toy transfer task, with a fairly toy pretraining dataset, but if the paper were accepted, I would say this is the strongest argument for it.

content.title: Response to Reviewer qZvu (Part1/2)
content.comment:
Thanks for your comments!


> Many results in this paper are fairly well established.

We compared different methods to find out the key influential factor to improve the ability of agents to communicate positional relationships. The intuition of using the random dataset is indeed not new and inspired by previous works, but we use two representative baseline datasets to show that the input variation between Speaker and Listener is more critical for communicating abstract information than adding noise and introducing stochasticity in the whole dataset. Besides, the main contribution of our work is exploring emergent communication about positional relationships and the effect of language transfer from referential games to MDP tasks. And we believe our research direction and proposed tasks are novel and our findings are meaningful.


> two-object positional relationships are a fairly limited concept, and the dataset itself is strictly a toy dataset. It would be interesting, for example, to set up a similar task with more realistic datasets

Since we explore the positional relationships and the language transfer from the referential game to MDP tasks, which are understudied in the existing literature, we need a more controllable environment for ease of exploration and analysis. (That means we can control the task difficulty, the number of combinations, and the kinds of positional relationships, we can generate datasets as we wish, and we can design a corresponding MDP task easily.) The two-object positional relationship is a simple but fundamental concept, which we think is suitable as a starting point for the research. And we conduct rather preliminary experiments with simple environments to focus on the viability and merits of learning positional relationships and language transfer to MDP tasks. Using realistic datasets, though very interesting, may introduce much complicated information that increases the difficulty of research at this stage. We have reached some valuable conclusions through the experiments, and we also listed the limitations in the last paragraph of Section 6. We will attempt to scale up the scope in the future.


> I am extremely surprised at the Figure 4 SimCLR results showing that using a better image encoder is unable to generalize...This also contradicts a long tradition in the literature

The test distribution is different from the training distribution since the combinations in the test set are unseen in training (e.g. "circle above square" is only in the test set, not the train set) (see the first paragraph in Section 3.3).

One reason to explain the result may be that after SimCLR pre-training, the image representations of different images generated by the same combination are very similar, so the effect of using the random dataset in the following referential game is diminished, since the target representations observed by Speaker and Listener are almost the same now.

From another perspective, the pre-trained encoders in advance separate different representations for different semantic information in the feature space, so the agents lose the environmental pressure to encode semantic information with emergent languages in the referential game, but can make use of some detailed information in the rich representation to accomplish the task. Then in the test set, though the pre-trained encoders can generate good representations for the new combinations, the agent language cannot generalize well to the new representations.

Using pre-trained image encoders is indeed common in the literature, but this result may imply one possible shortcoming of the common practice.

replying_to: Replying to Response to Reviewer qZvu (Part1/2)

content.title: Thanks for response
content.comment:
Thank you to authors for their detailed response to my review and for clarifying several questions I had about the paper!

Overall, however, my hesitation on accepting the paper remains the same, and is somewhat similar to reviewer k5EJ's hesitations about the lack of broader applicability to the emergent language community and beyond.

To reiterate my conclusion: this is a technically sound, reasonable investigation of one property of emergent language (two-object spatial relationships) applied to a single downstream task (a toy grid navigation task where the goal is to communicate spatial relationships), but the phenomenon (two-object spatial relationships) and the downstream tasks are, in my opinion, simply a little to toy to be broadly useful to other researchers in the field, as it stands right now. I can imagine a more substantial and exciting version of this paper where either more abstract linguistic/visual properties are studied beyond two-object relationships, and/or transfer evaluated on more realistic tasks that may be of interest to multi-agent/RL/vision+language researchers, like communication for more realistic navigation tasks (e.g. street navigation).

Note that I do not feel strongly about this decision and I do not necessarily want to gatekeep technically sound work from being published—thus I would have little objection if this paper were to be accepted. If it were to be accepted, the strongest argument would be investigating how emergent language can provide useful downstream transfer for more interesting MDP tasks, though again, the specific MDP task is fairly limited.

My opinion is one data point as to whether other researchers would find this work useful in its current state, but I am happy to be overridden and I think the overall decision is for the AC to make after synthesizing the various opinions collected by the reviewers here.

content.title: Thanks for your reply
content.comment:
Thanks for your reply.

For your hesitation, we would like to say that the more exciting version as you mentioned is also one of our future goals, as stated in Discussion. However, it is demanding to achieve these goals just through one paper since the gaps are still large (existing works have paid little attention to multiple objects and the application of the emergent language in realistic tasks) and we have to go step by step. Our finding in this paper is one important step, since it demonstrates the viability and the merits of our proposed points. And we hope the findings can inspire more researchers to pay attention to the direction and come up with more methods to approach the final goals.

content.title: Response to Reviewer qZvu (Part2/2)
content.comment:
> How are the distractors sampled in the batch? If distractor images are randomly sampled, then quite frequently agents would not actually need to communicate the specific positional relationship, right?

The distractor images are randomly sampled. Consciously sampling hard negatives may be an option, but increasing the distractor number can have similar effects, since there are very likely hard negatives in the distractors. We have 31 distractors out of totally 80 different combinations in the training set. (Besides, the random dataset also introduces the pressure for agents to communicate the positional relationship.)


> Dataset terms are a little unclear.

Thanks for the suggestions here. We will consider modifying the terms and adding some illustrations.


> How big is the fixed dataset? At a certain dataset size, will the fixed dataset be roughly equivalent to the variation dataset performance?

The combination number is the same in the three datasets (i.e., 100). So the size of the fixed dataset is exactly 100. We generate various image instances for each combination in variation dataset. If we see this as a kind of introducing stochasticity as adding random noise to images, the dataset size is the same (we also add random noises in the fixed dataset).


> Why are # of distractors changed from training to test time from 32 to 20? This feels like an arbitrary decision.

It is not an arbitrary decision. Following findings in previous works, we tend to use a larger number of distractors when training, and we find 32 performs best for all methods compared with smaller numbers such as 16 or 8. The distractor number at test time is 20 because we only have 20 different combinations in the test set, and we test on the full set to get stable and fair results.


> Did authors try additional finetuning of the speaker, using emergent communciation as the initialization point ?

We did not try this setting in the paper since we follow the ETL metric where the language is fixed to test the zero-shot generalization ability to different tasks, which can truly reveal the generality of language. We have now tried this setting, and find the performance is close to "rl-scratch" and worse than "ours", probably because the learned language is destroyed during the exploration of the training. The figure has been added to Appendix.

content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper presents a variation of the signalling game where the spatial relationship between two objects must be communicated via a discrete sequence of symbols.
Specifically, the experiments find that stochastically augmented dataset confers a number of benefits upon the resulting protocol which are not found in static datasets with less variation.
These advantages include better generalizability, more easily extractable information, and more compositionality.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
### Strengths
- [minor] The experiments show that stochasticity during training improves a handful of desirable properties about the emergent language system.
### Weaknesses
- [major] The evaluation does not sufficiently explore why this form of training is more effective or show that this effect is robust and generally applicable rather than specific to the specific environment.
- [minor] One of the major points of the paper seems to be the common wisdom that stochasticity/noise/randomization at training time can improve robustness and a number of other desirable properties, as a result.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
### Clarity
- The paper is easy enough to follow.
  The individual advantages of the proposed training method are clear, but how they all cohere to form a big-picture claim is less clear.
- Tables and figures that break the text (e.g., Table 1) are often distracting.
  I generally recommend using $\LaTeX$'s automatic figure placement.
### Quality
- The most positive aspect of this paper's quality is the strength of the empirical results.
  Generally speaking, the experiments show that using a stochastic training set is generally better including performance on unseen test data, compositionality (via toposim), and probing via a classification task.
- The breadth of experiments, though, takes away from the depth.
  Any one of these positive results merits further investigation (e.g., ablation studies) so as to try to get at the abstract principle which explains the random dataset's advantage over other configurations -- a brief conjecture is not sufficient.
  The resulting issue is that I finish the paper with some sense that stochasticity is important to emergent language but with no concrete sense of when, where, and how this will apply.
  - For example, it is intriguing that the random dataset significantly outperforms the contrastive learning features, but in order for this result to have an impact, there must some explanation of why this occurs.
- The environment selected is sufficient as a starting point and a testbed but would need to be bolstered with other environments to convincingly show that the effects of the random dataset are robust across environments.
  Ideally, some of these environments would be those used in previous work so as to have a direct point of reference.
  The space in the paper spent running additional, marginally related experiments would be better spent narrowing in on specific explanations or demonstrating the robustness of the effect.
### Novelty
- To a certain extent, the contributions of this paper rehash the general principle that certain kinds of noise in the training data can make a model more robust which comes with a handful of beneficial properties.
  Although this has not been explored extensively within emergent language, it is important to investigate and elucidate the specific aspects of emergent language which either require or improve further this kind of robustness.
  The empirical results of the paper point to such aspects, but they are not sufficiently explained.
- The environment is not new just by virtue of including relationality between objects (e.g., [TexRel](https://arxiv.org/abs/2105.12804v1) in addition to the other works cited in this paper).
  Similarly, other papers have introduced stochasticity and variation of speaker/listener observations, although this distinguishes itself by making such augmentations the focus.
- The motivation of the paper ought to be tied more concretely to the applications and goals of emergent language.
  The paper briefly discusses the importance of relationships between objects and how this aids in multi-step environments, but these concepts are still relatively abstract.
  It is not clear enough what kinds of problems in emergent language the techniques and results presented here will help solve.
### Reproducibility
- The specifics of the implementation are included, although it does appear that any code is or will be included.
content.summary_of_the_review:
I am recommending reject for this paper because despite the breadth and positive results of the experiments, the lack of depth makes it difficult to extrapolate general principles about emergent language and/or see how the results will enable various applications of emergent language.
In my estimation, presenting a new environment and training method, even if has some empirical merit, requires robust conceptual foundation and investigation to effectively tie it in with past and future emergent language research.


### Misc.
- 3.2 - Any reason for sampling from the categorical distribution parameterized by the softmax function instead of using Gumbel-Softmax sampling?
  Gumbel-Softmax is much more effective at backprop-able training when the output has to be discrete at test time.
- 5.1 - The first paragraph seems to be claiming that the emergent language agents are not robust to domain shift (i.e., fixed/variation at training time and random at test time).
  This is a pretty well established fact, so is this point just setting the stage for later points or is there some novelty and nuance here that I am missing?
- "overperforms" -> "outperforms"

content.title: Response to Reviewer k5Ej
content.comment:
Thanks for your comments!


> Weaknesses

The paper originated from a conjecture: if agents can communicate abstract information, their language may easily generalize to more complex tasks. To investigate this, we take positional relationships as an instance, because they are easy to control and integrate with MDP tasks. For learning such abstract information, we find the input variation is the key, better than noises or stochasticity in the whole dataset. More importantly, we demonstrate that communicating abstract information indeed induces better generalization to more complex tasks. Certainly, we cannot investigate all instances of abstract information in one paper, but our findings are meaningful and may shed light on future research in this direction.  

The reviewer seems to take the use of the random dataset as our main contribution, and the following questions are mainly about this, but this is not the case. 


> The individual advantages of the proposed training method are clear, but how they all cohere to form a big-picture claim is less clear.

Our experiments show that the input variation between Speaker and Listener is effective for agents' communication about abstract information, and this is also supported by previous works. So the training method might be useful for communication about other kinds of abstract information. 

> Tables and figures that break the text (e.g., Table 1) are often distracting.

Thanks for the suggestion. We will try to adjust. 

> no concrete sense of when, where, and how this will apply.

We compare with fixed dataset and variation dataset (and add random noise to images) exactly to show that just noise and stochasticity in the whole dataset is not effective enough where abstract information is involved, and the input variation between Speaker and Listener is more critical.

> The environment selected is sufficient as a starting point and a testbed but would need to be bolstered with other environments to convincingly show that the effects of the random dataset are robust across environments.

Our work is a starting point for exploring communicating positional relationships between objects and transferring language to MDP tasks, so we focus on the rather simple and controllable environment to mainly investigate the viability and merits of our proposed points. As mentioned in the last paragraph in Discussion, we will attempt to involve other environments in the future.

> The environment is not new just by virtue of including relationality between objects 

Relationality between objects is not entirely novel, but we think is a representative instance of abstracted information understudied in the literature. Moreover, positional relationships are controllable and easy to integrate with MDP tasks. 

> The motivation of the paper ought to be tied more concretely to the applications and goals of emergent language. 

Our motivation is that emergent language should serve as a general communication skill that can be used in various kinds of tasks other than the referential game. We start by training agents to learn positional relationships between objects to explore the language transfer towards multi-step MDP games, and show the viability and merits of the transfer of language. We hope this can exactly encourage more broad applications of emergent language.

replying_to: Replying to Response to Reviewer k5Ej

content.title: Strength of contributions
content.comment:
> The paper originated from a conjecture: if agents can communicate abstract
> information, their language may easily generalize to more complex tasks.
> [...] More importantly, we demonstrate that communicating abstract
> information indeed induces better generalization to more complex tasks.

The terms "abstract" and "complex" are key terms for this paper that require
better definition -- not simply a few extra sentences but a list of clear
criteria for what does and does not constitute "abstract information" as well
as what environment "complexity" means.  I do see how the paper works with an
intuitive notion of these concepts, but I think precise (and possibly formal)
definitions are important to the overall motivation and strength of the paper.

> Certainly, we cannot investigate all instances of abstract information in one
> paper, but our findings are meaningful and may shed light on future research
> in this direction.

I believe that one of the major problems for emergent language research has
been the integration of prior work into current work.  Part of the reason is
because a sizable portion of papers do not make a clear case for how the
contributions fit into future research.  Too often, I think the approach is
"the paper presents some interesting property that is intuitively important for
emergent language, so future work should be able to build on top of this", but
this is insufficient to argue for future usefulness since emergent language
research very open-ended and "basic" (i.e., not applied, yet).
  
> The reviewer seems to take the use of the random dataset as our main
> contribution, and the following questions are mainly about this, but this is
> not the case.

The "stochasticity" I refer to in my review was intended to include the
variation in speaker and listener perspectives.  Although distinct from
background variation and other sorts of noise, it falls under the same broad
category.

> Our work is a starting point for exploring communicating positional
> relationships between objects and transferring language to MDP tasks, so we
> focus on the rather simple and controllable environment to mainly investigate
> the viability and merits of our proposed points. As mentioned in the last
> paragraph in Discussion, we will attempt to involve other environments in the
> future.

I do understand why this paper uses a simple environment, but I typically look
for one of two things in an emergent language making empirical claims:
- A simple environment which demonstrates the principal and a robust analysis
  of why this is occurring.
- A handful of more realistic environments which shows that the phenomenon is
  robust across environments.

Given that this paper focuses on a simple environment, I had hoped to see
a better explanation for the "why" of the phenomenon.

> Our motivation is that emergent language should serve as a general
> communication skill that can be used in various kinds of tasks other than the
> referential game. We start by training agents to learn positional relationships
> between objects to explore the language transfer towards multi-step MDP games,
> and show the viability and merits of the transfer of language. We hope this can
> exactly encourage more broad applications of emergent language.

See second response of this comment.

content.title: Response
content.comment:
Thanks for your reply.

> The terms "abstract" and "complex" are key terms for this paper that require better definition

As stated in our paper (the second paragraph in Introduction), we refer to tasks with more realistic settings other than the referential game as "complex", which is indeed a general statement since most existing works are only limited to the referential games and we want to break through. And we also clearly refer to the multi-step MDP tasks as the "complex" tasks that we focus on in the paper.

“Abstract information" itself contains many kinds of information, but we only explore the positional relationships in our paper, which we think is a clear definition (positional relationships vs. absolute positions). We believe our results may be applicable to other kinds of abstract information (and we list some examples in the paper). But giving out a clear definition for "abstract" is beyond the scope of our paper. 

> this is insufficient to argue for future usefulness since emergent language research very open-ended and "basic" (i.e., not applied, yet).

We think our exploration of two-object positional relationships can encourage future work to turn the gaze away from single objects, our findings of the critical effect of the input variation between Speaker and Listener can inspire future research that also studies under the scope of referential games (just like how we are inspired by previous works), and our results that show the viability and advantages of language transfer from referential games to MDP tasks can inspire future studies to pay attention to the general capacity of emergent communication and the application of emergent language in more realistic settings.

We provide new ideas and possibilities for future research directions, but it is not our responsibility to direct how specifically future research utilizes these contributions. As you mentioned, emergent language research is "basic", so it is unreasonable to expect immediate future usefulness.

> Given that this paper focuses on a simple environment, I had hoped to see a better explanation for the "why" of the phenomenon.

For "phenomenon", if you refer to the effect of using the random dataset, the intuition is clear in the paper that the stronger environmental pressure pushes agents to communicate abstract information so as to get rewards. The effect is also demonstrated in previous works in other environments, so it is "robust across environments", and we verify that the effect is more critical when positional relationships are involved in the environment.

If you refer to the effect of language transfer to multi-step MDP tasks, we explain in the second to last paragraph of Section 5.3.2 that the phenomenon is in line with previous symbolic representation research that the conceptual abstraction provided by symbolic representation can promote data-efficient learning, which is the main obstacle of deep learning.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper focuses on the domain of emergent communication and investigates whether communicating neural agents can express spatial relationships between multiple in a referential game. Firstly, the paper demonstrates that input variation between Speaker and Listener’s inputs is necessary to develop productive languages. Next, the authors report a set of experiments that show how emergent languages can generalize well to solve different tasks. In particular, they demonstrate that the emergent communication-pretrained language generalizes to a complex multi-step MDP task where the positional relationship is important. Moreover, its performs significantly better than learning the language directly during the training or providing raw input to the Listener.
content.summary_of_the_review: I find the paper novel and results convincing & encouraging. My main concern is the performance of the SimCLR baseline.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 4: The contributions are significant, and do not exist in prior works.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.

content.title: Response to Reviewer y3tf
content.comment:
Thanks for your comments!

> The results of the SimCLR experiments are very puzzling...I would encourage authors to clarify this.

In our experiments the pre-trained SimCLR model is frozen, and we have made it clear in the revision.

We also thought the SimCLR model would be helpful before the experiment, but the results show the generalization problem. One reason to explain the result may be that after SimCLR pre-training, the image representations of different images generated by the same combination are very similar, so the effect of using the random dataset in the following referential game is diminished, since the target representations observed by Speaker and Listener is almost the same now. From another perspective, the pre-trained encoders in advance separate different representations for different semantic information in the feature space, so the agents lose the environmental pressure to encode semantic information with emergent languages in the referential game, but can make use of some detailed information in the rich representation to accomplish the task. Then in the test set, though the pre-trained encoders can generate good representations for the new combinations, the agent language cannot generalize well to the new representations.


> The 'Visual representation' metric is similar to the one proposed by (Dessi et al. 2021).

Thanks for pointing that out. We have made it clear in the revision.
